questions.title: var, let, and const: scope and reassignment
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between declaring a variable with var, let, and const in JavaScript, and why do most modern style guides recommend avoiding var entirely?
questions.modelAnswer: var is function-scoped and is hoisted to the top of its enclosing function with an initial value of undefined, which means it can be accidentally read or reassigned before the line that declares it, and it leaks out of if/for blocks into the surrounding function. let and const are both block-scoped -- confined to the nearest { } -- and are hoisted into a 'temporal dead zone' where referencing them before their declaration throws an error instead of silently returning undefined, which surfaces bugs immediately instead of hiding them. const additionally prevents the variable binding itself from being reassigned after its initial assignment, though it does not make an object or array referenced by a const variable immutable -- its contents can still be changed, only the variable itself can't be pointed at a new value.
questions.professionalAnswer: I avoid var almost entirely at this point. The real problem with it is that it's function-scoped, not block-scoped, so a variable declared inside an if block or a for loop is still visible and reassignable outside that block, which has caused me real bugs where a loop variable leaked further than I expected. let and const fix that by actually respecting the block they're declared in. I default to const for everything, and only reach for let when I know a variable genuinely needs to be reassigned later -- that habit alone catches a surprising number of 'wait, why did this change' bugs, because the compiler stops me from reassigning something I didn't mean to be reassignable. The one thing I'm careful to explain to someone newer is that const doesn't freeze an object -- const user = { name: 'a' } still lets you do user.name = 'b', it just stops you from doing user = {} entirely.
commonMistakes: Declaring a loop counter with var inside a for loop and being surprised it's still accessible after the loop ends
Assuming const makes an object or array fully immutable, when it only prevents reassigning the variable binding itself
Reading a let/const variable before its declaration and being confused by the resulting error instead of recognizing the temporal dead zone
Mixing var and let/const in the same codebase without a clear reason, making scope harder to reason about
keyPoints: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let/const are block-scoped
let/const in a temporal dead zone throw if referenced before declaration, surfacing bugs earlier than var's silent undefined
const prevents reassigning the variable binding, not mutating an object/array it points to
Modern style guides default to const, use let only when reassignment is genuinely needed, and avoid var

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains function-scope vs. block-scope
Correctly explains const's reassignment-vs-mutation distinction
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Function declarations vs. arrow functions, and this
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between a regular function declaration and an arrow function in JavaScript, especially around how each one handles the `this` keyword?
questions.modelAnswer: A regular function gets its own `this`, determined dynamically by how it's actually called -- as a method on an object, `this` is that object; called plainly, `this` is undefined (in strict mode/modules) or the global object otherwise. An arrow function does not have its own `this` at all; instead it captures `this` lexically from whatever scope it was defined in, and that binding never changes no matter how the arrow function is later called or passed around. This makes arrow functions well suited as callbacks inside a method where you want `this` to keep referring to the surrounding object, but poorly suited as an object's own method shorthand, since an arrow function defined directly as a property has no enclosing `this` of its own to inherit other than whatever was outside the object literal.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about it: a regular function asks 'who called me?' every time to figure out `this`, while an arrow function never asks that question at all -- it just uses whatever `this` already meant in the surrounding code where it was written, permanently. That's exactly why I reach for arrow functions for callbacks inside a class method -- say, inside a method that sets up a setTimeout -- because I want `this` inside that callback to still mean the class instance, not get reset by how setTimeout happens to invoke it. The mistake I watch for is using an arrow function as an actual object method, like `const wallet = { balance: 10, log: () => console.log(this.balance) }` -- that arrow function's `this` isn't the wallet object at all, it's whatever `this` was in the outer scope, so it won't do what you'd expect.
commonMistakes: Defining an object's own method as an arrow function and expecting `this` to refer to that object
Using a regular function as a callback inside a class method and losing the intended `this` binding when it's invoked
Assuming arrow functions are just shorter syntax with no actual behavioral difference around `this`
Not knowing arrow functions can't be used as constructors (no `new` support)
keyPoints: Regular functions get their own `this`, determined by how they're called at call time
Arrow functions have no own `this`; they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope, fixed at definition time
Arrow functions are good for callbacks that need the outer `this`; bad as a direct object method
Arrow functions also lack their own arguments object and cannot be used with `new`

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains dynamic vs. lexical `this`
Gives a correct example of when each is appropriate

questions.title: What the event loop actually does
questions.prompt: JavaScript is often described as 'single-threaded but non-blocking.' What does the event loop actually do that makes that possible, and why does that matter when your code is waiting on a network call?
questions.modelAnswer: The call stack runs synchronous code one function at a time on a single thread. When code starts an asynchronous operation -- a timer, a file read, a network call -- that operation is handed off to the surrounding runtime (the browser or Node's libuv) to actually carry out, and the JavaScript thread moves on immediately rather than waiting. Once that operation finishes, its callback (or the resolution of a Promise) is placed into a queue, and the event loop's job is to continuously check whether the call stack is currently empty, and if so, pull the next item off that queue and run it. This is what lets a single thread stay responsive during a slow network call: it doesn't sit frozen waiting for the response, it goes on to handle other work, and only comes back to the network call's result once that result is actually ready.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as a thread that refuses to just sit and wait. When I call an API or hit a blockchain node's RPC endpoint, that network call takes real time -- maybe a few hundred milliseconds -- and if JavaScript's single thread just blocked on that, nothing else in the app could happen for that whole window. Instead, the runtime hands that network call off outside the main thread, the JS thread is immediately free to do other things, and when the response actually comes back, its callback gets queued up and the event loop picks it up the next time the call stack is clear. The practical upside for something like checking many users' transaction statuses: I'm not actually running those checks one at a time waiting for each network round trip -- they're all in flight at once, and the single thread just handles each one's result as it arrives.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'single-threaded' means JavaScript can't do multiple things at once at all, missing that I/O is offloaded elsewhere
Thinking the event loop runs code in parallel on multiple threads rather than one thread picking up queued callbacks
Not connecting the non-blocking model to why many concurrent network calls (like multiple RPC requests) don't freeze the app
Confusing a slow synchronous loop (CPU-bound) with a slow network call (I/O-bound) as if both behave the same way
keyPoints: The call stack runs synchronous code on a single thread, one function at a time
Async operations (I/O, timers, network calls) are handed off to the runtime instead of blocking the thread
Completed async operations' callbacks are queued, and the event loop runs them once the call stack is empty
This lets one thread stay responsive during slow network calls, which matters for things like RPC calls to a blockchain node

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the call stack, offloading, and the queue
Correctly connects it to a real network-call scenario
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What async/await actually is under the hood
questions.prompt: If async/await isn't really a different way of doing asynchronous JavaScript, what is it actually syntactic sugar over, and what does the await keyword actually do to the function's execution?
questions.modelAnswer: async/await is syntactic sugar built entirely on top of Promises -- it doesn't introduce a new asynchronous mechanism, it just gives Promise-based code a more linear, synchronous-looking shape. Marking a function async guarantees that function always returns a Promise, even if its body just returns a plain value (which gets automatically wrapped). Inside an async function, the await keyword pauses that function's own execution at that line until the Promise it's given actually settles -- it does not block the rest of the program or the single JS thread, only the execution of that specific async function -- and then resumes with the Promise's resolved value, or throws the rejection as a catchable error if the Promise rejected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of async/await as just a nicer way to write .then() chains without actually changing what's happening underneath. When I write `const result = await getBalance(address)`, that's functionally equivalent to `getBalance(address).then(result => ...)`, just written so it reads top-to-bottom instead of nested in callbacks. The part people sometimes get wrong is thinking await blocks the whole program -- it doesn't, it only pauses the one async function it's inside of; everything else in the app keeps running normally while that function is paused waiting on its Promise. And since an async function always returns a Promise no matter what, calling an async function from outside still needs its own await or .then() to actually get the real value out of it.
commonMistakes: Believing await blocks the entire program/thread rather than just pausing the current async function
Forgetting an async function always returns a Promise, and trying to use its return value directly without awaiting the call
Not realizing async/await and .then() chains are interchangeable, equally valid ways of handling the same underlying Promise
Omitting try/catch around an await, missing that a rejected awaited Promise throws a normal catchable error
keyPoints: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises, not a separate asynchronous mechanism
An async function always returns a Promise, even for a plain returned value
await pauses only the current async function's execution, not the whole program, until its Promise settles
A rejected awaited Promise throws, and should be handled with try/catch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies async/await as sugar over Promises
Correctly explains what await does to execution
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What TypeScript actually adds over plain JavaScript
questions.prompt: TypeScript code still ultimately runs as JavaScript. So what does TypeScript actually give you that plain JavaScript doesn't, and at what point does that checking actually happen?
questions.modelAnswer: TypeScript adds a static type system that the TypeScript compiler checks entirely at compile time, before the code is ever run -- it analyzes declared and inferred types across the codebase and flags mismatches (passing a string where a number was expected, calling a method that doesn't exist on a given type) as compile errors. Those types exist only during this compilation step; once the compiler transpiles .ts files down to plain .js, all the type annotations are erased and the resulting JavaScript that actually runs has no type information left in it at all -- TypeScript's checking is a development-time safety net, not a runtime guarantee. For something like blockchain development, this is particularly valuable because deploying or interacting with a smart contract is slow and can cost real gas, so catching a mistake like passing an address where an amount was expected before ever running the code is worth far more than finding it live.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put it simply: TypeScript catches a category of mistakes before the code ever runs, instead of finding out about them in production. The compiler reads my type annotations -- a parameter declared as `string`, an interface describing what a transaction object looks like -- and if I try to pass the wrong shape of data somewhere, it refuses to compile and tells me exactly where. The thing I make sure people understand is that this checking only happens during that compile step; the actual JavaScript that ends up running in the browser or in Node has none of those types left in it anymore, so TypeScript isn't protecting me against bad data that shows up at runtime, like an API unexpectedly returning the wrong shape -- for that I still need real runtime validation, not just a type annotation.
commonMistakes: Assuming TypeScript's types are checked at runtime, not just during compilation
Using 'any' liberally, which quietly opts out of the type checking TypeScript is supposed to provide
Believing a TypeScript type annotation on external data (like a parsed API response) guarantees that data actually has that shape
Thinking TypeScript changes how the code executes, rather than just checking it before compiling it down to plain JavaScript
keyPoints: TypeScript adds static type checking performed by the compiler, at compile time
Types are erased during compilation; the emitted JavaScript has no type information at runtime
This catches many mistakes before code ever runs, which matters especially for gas-costing or hard-to-debug-live blockchain calls
TypeScript doesn't replace runtime validation for genuinely external/untrusted data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains compile-time checking vs. runtime erasure
Gives a concrete benefit relevant to this domain
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What a blockchain actually is, beyond 'a database'
questions.prompt: A friend asks you what a blockchain actually is, beyond just saying 'it's a database.' How would you explain it, and what specifically makes it different from a normal company's database?
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger -- a growing list of records (blocks) -- that is replicated across many independent computers (nodes) rather than stored on servers owned by a single company, with each block cryptographically linked to the one before it so the sequence can't be silently rewritten. A normal company database is centralized: one organization owns the servers, controls who can read or write to it, and can unilaterally edit or delete records at will. A blockchain removes that single point of control -- no one node's copy is automatically authoritative, and changing the agreed-upon history requires convincing the network's consensus mechanism, not just editing one party's own copy -- which is the actual property people mean when they call it 'trustless' or decentralized.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with what's the same: yes, at its core it's just a list of records, similar to a database. What's actually different is who controls it. A company's database lives on that company's own servers, and if they decide to change a record, they just do it -- there's no one to stop them. A blockchain is instead copied across thousands of independent computers run by unrelated people, and each new entry is cryptographically tied to everything that came before it, so there isn't one 'owner' who can quietly edit old history -- any change has to be accepted by the whole network's agreed-upon rules, not just typed into one company's system. That's the actual point of a blockchain: not that it's a fancier database, but that no single party is in charge of it.
commonMistakes: Describing a blockchain as 'just a database' without naming what structurally makes it different
Not mentioning that many independent nodes hold copies of the same ledger, rather than one central owner
Confusing decentralization with 'no rules' rather than 'rules enforced by consensus instead of by one party'
Assuming every blockchain is public/permissionless, without acknowledging private/permissioned variants exist
keyPoints: A blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger replicated across many independent nodes
Each block cryptographically links to the previous one, making the sequence hard to silently rewrite
A normal database is centrally owned and editable by one party; a blockchain has no single controlling party
Changing agreed history requires the network's consensus, not just one party's own edit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a blockchain structurally
Correctly contrasts it with a centralized database
Clarity of explanation for a non-technical audience

questions.title: Why hashing is what makes a blockchain tamper-evident
questions.prompt: What is a cryptographic hash function, and specifically how does chaining each block's hash to the previous block's hash make tampering with old data detectable?
questions.modelAnswer: A cryptographic hash function takes any input, of any size, and deterministically produces a fixed-size output (the hash) -- the same input always produces the same hash, but even a tiny, one-character change to the input produces a completely different, unrelated-looking hash (the avalanche effect). In a blockchain, each block stores the hash of the previous block's contents as part of its own data. If someone goes back and alters anything inside an old block, that block's hash changes as a direct consequence -- but the next block in the chain already recorded the old, original hash as 'the previous block's hash,' so that recorded value no longer matches the altered block's new actual hash. That mismatch is immediately checkable by anyone, which is what makes tampering with old data detectable rather than silent: the altered block would have to also have every single subsequent block's stored hash rewritten to match, cascading all the way to the current tip of the chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain a hash function as something that turns any input into a short fixed-length fingerprint, where changing even one character of the input completely scrambles that fingerprint into something unrecognizable. The clever part of a blockchain is that each block includes the previous block's fingerprint as part of its own data. So if I go back and change something in block 100, block 100's fingerprint changes -- but block 101 already recorded what block 100's fingerprint was supposed to be, and now it doesn't match. Anyone checking can immediately see that mismatch. To actually get away with the tamper, I'd have to also rewrite block 101's recorded hash to match my new version of block 100, which breaks block 102's record of block 101's hash, and so on all the way to the newest block -- which is exactly the cascading, practically-impossible-at-scale problem that makes old blocks effectively tamper-evident.
commonMistakes: Describing hashing as encryption (reversible), rather than a one-way, irreversible transformation
Not explaining the avalanche effect -- that a tiny input change produces a completely different hash
Missing that it's specifically the chaining of each block's hash into the next block that creates tamper-evidence, not hashing alone
Assuming tampering is literally impossible rather than detectable and requiring an impractical cascading rewrite to hide
keyPoints: A hash function deterministically maps any input to a fixed-size output; tiny input changes produce a totally different hash
Each block stores the previous block's hash as part of its own data
Altering an old block changes its hash, which no longer matches what the next block already recorded
Hiding a tamper requires rewriting every subsequent block's hash all the way to the current tip -- the actual source of tamper-evidence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a hash function does
Correctly explains the chaining mechanism and why it's detectable
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Proof of Work vs. Proof of Stake, in plain terms
questions.prompt: What problem is a consensus mechanism like Proof of Work or Proof of Stake actually solving, and what's the practical difference between how the two decide who gets to add the next block?
questions.modelAnswer: A consensus mechanism solves the problem of letting a decentralized network made up of many mutually distrusting, unrelated participants agree on a single, legitimate next block -- and on the ledger's history overall -- without any central authority making that call. Proof of Work has participants (miners) compete to solve a computationally expensive, trial-and-error puzzle; whoever finds a valid solution first earns the right to propose the next block, and that real spent computational effort (and electricity) is what makes it costly to cheat or rewrite history. Proof of Stake instead has participants (validators) lock up a quantity of the network's own cryptocurrency as collateral ('stake'), and the network selects who proposes and attests to the next block roughly in proportion to how much they have staked; a validator caught acting dishonestly can have part or all of their stake taken away ('slashed'), which replaces burning real-world energy with risking locked-up capital as the deterrent, at a small fraction of the energy cost.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what problem both are solving first: with no central referee, how do thousands of strangers running independent nodes agree on exactly one 'next block' instead of everyone proposing their own and causing chaos? Proof of Work answers that by making it expensive to get the right to propose a block -- you have to actually burn real computing power solving a puzzle, and whoever solves it first wins that right, which also makes rewriting old blocks prohibitively expensive since you'd have to redo all that work. Proof of Stake answers the same question differently -- instead of burning energy, validators put up their own crypto as a bond, get chosen to propose/validate roughly based on how much they've staked, and lose that stake if they're caught cheating. The practical difference I always mention: PoS uses a small fraction of the energy PoW does, which is specifically why Ethereum switched to it during the Merge.
commonMistakes: Describing PoW/PoS as competing cryptocurrencies rather than as consensus mechanisms a network can use
Not explaining what problem consensus actually solves (agreeing on one legitimate next block/history without a central authority)
Confusing staking (locking collateral) with mining (spending computational work) when describing either mechanism
Missing the actual deterrent in each: wasted real-world energy in PoW vs. slashable locked collateral in PoS
keyPoints: Consensus lets a decentralized, mutually distrusting network agree on the next block without a central authority
PoW: miners compete via computationally expensive puzzle-solving; winner proposes the next block
PoS: validators lock up stake as collateral; selection is roughly proportional to stake, with slashing for dishonesty
PoS achieves similar security guarantees at a small fraction of PoW's energy cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the problem consensus mechanisms solve
Correctly explains both PoW and PoS mechanics

questions.title: What a wallet's public/private key pair actually controls
questions.prompt: A crypto wallet doesn't actually 'store' your coins the way a physical wallet stores cash. What does a wallet's private key actually control, and what is a wallet address derived from?
questions.modelAnswer: Balances live on the blockchain's own shared ledger, associated with an address -- not inside any particular wallet app or device. A wallet's private key is a secret number that lets its holder cryptographically sign transactions, mathematically proving the authority to move funds associated with a given address, without ever having to reveal the private key itself to anyone. The public key is mathematically derived from the private key (and can be shared safely, since it can't be used to reverse-derive the private key), and the wallet address itself is typically a further hashed and shortened representation derived from that public key. Whoever possesses the private key has complete and irreversible control over whatever is associated with that address on-chain -- there is no password reset: lose the private key and the funds are permanently inaccessible, and expose it and anyone who sees it can sign transactions exactly as if they were the real owner.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd correct the mental model first: a wallet app doesn't actually hold your coins inside it, the way a physical wallet holds cash. The actual balance just lives on the blockchain, attached to an address. What the wallet app is really holding onto, and protecting, is your private key -- a secret number that lets you sign a transaction proving you're authorized to move whatever's associated with that address, without that secret ever having to leave your device or be shown to anyone. The public key and the address itself are both just derived mathematically from that private key, in a one-way direction -- you can get the public key and address from the private key, but not the other way around, which is exactly what keeps it safe to share your address publicly. The one thing I always emphasize: there's no 'forgot password' here. If the private key is lost, whatever's at that address is gone permanently; if it's exposed to someone else, they now have exactly the same control over it that you do.
commonMistakes: Describing a wallet as 'storing' coins, rather than storing the private key that controls on-chain balances
Assuming the address is the same thing as the public key, rather than a further derived (usually hashed) value
Not understanding the one-way derivation (private key -> public key -> address), and thinking it could be reversed
Underestimating that losing a private key is permanent and irreversible, unlike a forgotten account password
keyPoints: Balances exist on the blockchain's ledger tied to an address, not stored inside the wallet app itself
The private key signs transactions to prove authority to move funds, without ever being revealed
The public key is mathematically derived from the private key; the address is typically derived (hashed) from the public key
Derivation is one-way; losing the private key means permanent loss, and exposing it means total loss of control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that balances live on-chain, not in the wallet
Correctly explains the private/public key/address relationship
Correctly emphasizes the irreversibility of losing/exposing the private key

questions.title: What gas on Ethereum actually pays for
questions.prompt: What is 'gas' on Ethereum actually a measurement of, and why does a simple ETH transfer cost less gas than calling a function on a smart contract?
questions.modelAnswer: Gas measures the computational work a transaction requires every node on the network to perform in order to execute and validate it. Every low-level operation the EVM performs (adding two numbers, reading from storage, writing to storage) has its own fixed gas cost, and a transaction's total gas used is simply the sum of all the operations it actually triggers while executing. A plain ETH transfer only has to perform a minimal, fixed set of operations -- essentially updating two account balances -- so its gas cost is small and predictable. Calling a function on a smart contract can execute arbitrary logic defined by that contract's code: it might loop, read and write multiple storage slots, call other contracts, or run complex calculations, and every one of those additional operations adds its own gas cost on top, which is why contract interactions are routinely far more expensive than a simple transfer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe gas as a receipt for computational work, not just an arbitrary fee. Every single operation the EVM does -- adding numbers, storing a value, reading a value -- has its own fixed gas price baked into the protocol, and the total gas for a transaction is just the sum of whatever operations it actually ends up running. A plain ETH transfer does almost nothing computationally -- it updates two balances and that's basically it -- so its gas cost is small and consistent every time. Calling a contract function is a completely different story, because that function's code can do anything -- loop over an array, write to several storage variables, call into another contract -- and each of those operations tacks its own gas cost on. That's exactly why I'd never assume two transactions cost the same just because they're both 'one transaction' -- the actual work being done underneath is what gas is measuring.
commonMistakes: Treating gas as a flat, arbitrary fee rather than a measurement of the actual computational work performed
Assuming all transactions cost roughly the same gas regardless of what they actually do
Not connecting storage writes specifically to high gas cost, since writing to contract storage is one of the more expensive EVM operations
Confusing gas (the unit of computational work) with gas price (what you pay per unit) and the total fee (gas used × gas price)
keyPoints: Gas measures the computational work required to execute and validate a transaction
Every EVM operation has its own fixed gas cost; total gas is the sum of all operations actually executed
A plain ETH transfer performs minimal, fixed work (updating two balances), so it costs little gas
A contract function call can trigger arbitrary logic (loops, storage writes, other calls), each adding its own gas cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what gas measures
Correctly explains why contract calls cost more than transfers

questions.title: Filter and transform an array of transactions
questions.prompt: Given an array of transaction objects, each with an amount and a confirmed field, write a single chained expression using array methods that returns an array of just the amounts of the confirmed transactions, each amount doubled.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic approach chains .filter() and .map(): .filter() first walks the array and keeps only the elements where confirmed is true, returning a new, shorter array without mutating the original; .map() then walks that filtered array and transforms each remaining element -- here, multiplying amount by 2 -- returning a new array of just those transformed values. Filtering before mapping is the natural order here since there's no reason to transform transactions that are about to be discarded anyway.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for filter().map() without a second thought: transactions.filter(tx => tx.confirmed).map(tx => tx.amount * 2). I like that each step reads like a sentence -- 'keep the confirmed ones, then double their amounts' -- and neither step touches the original array, so I'm not worried about side effects elsewhere in the code that might still rely on the original list. I'd avoid writing this with a manual forEach and a pushed-into array; it works, but it's more code, introduces a mutable accumulator I have to manage myself, and reads less clearly than the chain.
commonMistakes: Using forEach with a manually managed accumulator array instead of chaining filter and map
Mapping before filtering, doing unnecessary transformation work on entries that get discarded anyway
Mutating the original transactions array instead of relying on filter/map's non-mutating return values
Forgetting that filter's callback must return a boolean, not the value itself
keyPoints: filter() returns a new array containing only elements that pass the test, without mutating the original
map() returns a new array of transformed values, one per element of the array it's called on
Chaining filter().map() in that order avoids wasted work transforming elements about to be discarded
Neither method mutates the array it's called on

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses filter to keep only confirmed transactions
Correctly uses map to double the amount
Chains them cleanly without mutation

questions.title: Write an async function with proper error handling
questions.prompt: Write an async function getBlockNumber(provider) that calls provider.getBlockNumber() (which returns a Promise), awaits the result, and returns it -- but if the call throws, logs a clear error message and returns null instead of letting the error crash the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: The awaited call needs to be wrapped in a try/catch inside the async function: the try block awaits provider.getBlockNumber() and returns its resolved value on success; the catch block runs if that Promise rejects, logging a clear, specific message (including the actual error) and returning null instead of letting the rejection propagate up uncaught. Returning null (rather than letting the error throw) gives the caller a predictable, checkable failure value instead of forcing every caller to also wrap this call in its own try/catch.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it with the try/catch directly around the awaited call: async function getBlockNumber(provider) { try { return await provider.getBlockNumber(); } catch (err) { console.error('Failed to fetch block number:', err.message); return null; } }. I specifically log the actual error message rather than a generic 'something went wrong,' because when this fails in practice -- usually a network hiccup or a bad RPC endpoint -- I want to know why without having to reproduce it. Returning null instead of re-throwing is a deliberate choice here too: it means whoever calls getBlockNumber can just check `if (blockNumber === null)` instead of being forced to wrap every single call site in its own try/catch.
commonMistakes: Omitting try/catch entirely, leaving a rejected promise as an unhandled rejection
Catching the error but still implicitly returning undefined instead of the specified null
Logging a generic message with no actual error detail, making the failure hard to diagnose later
Re-throwing the error from the catch block, defeating the purpose of handling it inside this function
keyPoints: try/catch around the awaited call is the standard way to handle a rejected Promise in async/await code
The catch block should log a specific, useful message, not a generic one
Returning null on failure gives callers a predictable value to check instead of requiring their own try/catch
An async function's return value inside try is what the function resolves to on success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly awaits inside a try block
Correctly catches and logs a clear error message
Returns null on failure as specified

questions.title: Write a TypeScript interface for a transaction
questions.prompt: Write a TypeScript interface named Transaction that describes an object with a string from address, a string to address, a numeric value (in wei, as a number for simplicity), and an optional string memo field.
questions.modelAnswer: An interface declares the required shape of an object: from and to are declared as string, value is declared as number, and memo is declared as an optional property using the ? modifier after its name, meaning an object can satisfy this interface whether or not it includes a memo at all. Any object assigned a Transaction type must include from, to, and value with matching types, while memo may be present and must be a string if it is.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write: interface Transaction { from: string; to: string; value: number; memo?: string; }. The thing I'm careful about is that question mark on memo -- without it, TypeScript would require every single Transaction object to include a memo field, even when there isn't one to give, which doesn't match how this data actually looks in practice. I'd also resist the temptation to type value as any just because wei amounts can get large -- number works for this simplified example, though in a real project I'd flag that genuine on-chain values often need BigInt or a dedicated big-number type since they can exceed what a JS number can represent precisely.
commonMistakes: Making memo required instead of optional, forcing every object to include it even when there's nothing to say
Using 'any' or omitting a type for one of the fields instead of giving it a specific type
Confusing optional property syntax (fieldName?: type) with allowing undefined as an explicit type (fieldName: type | undefined)

questions.title: Write a constructor that sets the contract's owner

Inside it, msg.sender refers to whichever address actually sent the deployment transaction, so assigning owner = msg.sender there permanently records the deployer's address into the owner state variable. Because owner is a stored state variable rather than something re-read from msg.sender later, it correctly keeps pointing to the original deployer even when other, later functions are called by different addresses.

questions.title: Write a for loop that sums an array
questions.prompt: Write a Solidity function totalOf(uint256[] memory amounts) that uses a for loop to add up every value in the amounts array and returns the total.
questions.modelAnswer: A for loop initializes a uint256 index at 0, continues while that index is less than amounts.length, and increments it each pass, adding amounts[i] into a running total variable on every iteration; the function returns total once the loop finishes. Since the function doesn't read or write any contract state, only its own parameters, it can be marked pure rather than view. It's worth noting that looping over the full length of a caller-supplied array costs gas proportional to the array's size, so a very large array passed into a function like this can become expensive or even risk hitting a gas limit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write: function totalOf(uint256[] memory amounts) public pure returns (uint256) { uint256 total = 0; for (uint256 i = 0; i < amounts.length; i++) { total += amounts[i]; } return total; }. I marked it pure rather than view since it doesn't touch any contract storage at all, only its own parameter -- that's a step beyond view, which still allows reading state. The thing I'd flag as a real-world gotcha here: this loop's gas cost scales directly with how long the amounts array actually is, so if this were called with an array controlled by an untrusted caller and no size limit, it could become unexpectedly expensive or even revert from running out of gas -- that's a genuine gas-awareness habit, not just a syntax detail.

questions.title: Debug a lost `this` inside a callback
questions.prompt: A Wallet class has a method logBalance() that logs this.balance, but when it's passed directly as a callback -- setTimeout(wallet.logBalance, 1000) -- it logs undefined instead of the actual balance. What's actually going wrong, and what are two different ways to fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Passing wallet.logBalance by reference detaches the function from the wallet object entirely -- it's now just a plain function value, with no memory of which object it was originally a method on. When setTimeout later calls that function on its own, this inside it is no longer bound to wallet (it's undefined in strict mode/ES modules, or the global object otherwise), so this.balance reads as undefined. Two fixes: wrap the call in an arrow function so the method is actually invoked on wallet -- setTimeout(() => wallet.logBalance(), 1000) -- which preserves the correct call-site binding, or explicitly bind the method to wallet before passing it -- setTimeout(wallet.logBalance.bind(wallet), 1000) -- which permanently locks this to wallet regardless of how the resulting function is later called.
questions.professionalAnswer: The bug is that passing wallet.logBalance by itself strips away the connection to wallet -- functions in JavaScript don't carry their object with them just because they were defined as a method; this is determined by how a function is actually called, not where it was defined. Once setTimeout calls that detached function on its own later, there's no wallet object involved in the call at all, so this.balance is undefined. I'd fix it either by wrapping it in an arrow function -- setTimeout(() => wallet.logBalance(), 1000) -- so the method call actually happens on wallet when it runs, or by using .bind(wallet) up front -- setTimeout(wallet.logBalance.bind(wallet), 1000) -- which creates a new function permanently locked to that this, no matter how it's later invoked. I'd reach for bind specifically when the function might get passed around multiple times and I want the binding to be permanent rather than re-wrapped every time.

questions.title: Diagnose an unhandled promise rejection crashing the process
questions.prompt: Your Node script calls fetchBalance(address) (which returns a Promise) without await or .catch(), and sometime later the process crashes with an UnhandledPromiseRejectionWarning. What's actually happening, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Calling a function that returns a Promise without awaiting it or attaching a .catch() means nothing in the code is actually listening for that Promise's outcome -- if the underlying network call fails and the Promise rejects, that rejection has nowhere to go. In modern Node, an unhandled rejection like this isn't just logged as a warning and ignored -- it can actually crash the process, specifically because an unhandled asynchronous failure is treated as a serious, unaddressed bug rather than something safe to silently drop. The fix is to actually handle the rejection: either await the call inside an async function wrapped in try/catch, or chain .catch(err => ...) directly onto the returned Promise so the failure path is explicitly handled.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's actually happening is that fetchBalance(address) is being called in a 'fire and forget' way -- nothing awaits it and nothing catches it, so if the network call it makes ever fails, that rejected Promise has no handler attached to it anywhere. Node treats that as a real problem, not a harmless omission, and in current versions it can bring the whole process down rather than quietly logging a warning forever. The fix is just to actually handle it -- either await fetchBalance(address) inside an async function with a surrounding try/catch, or chain .catch(err => console.error('Failed to fetch balance:', err)) directly onto the call if I'm intentionally not awaiting it. The deeper habit this points to: any time a function returns a Promise and its result (or failure) actually matters, it needs to be awaited or caught -- never just called and left alone.

questions.title: Diagnose a working-on-my-machine npm dependency issue
questions.prompt: A teammate pulls your project, runs npm install, and their app crashes with an error that doesn't happen on your machine. You both have the same package.json. What's the most likely cause, and what command/file would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: package.json typically declares dependencies as version ranges (like ^5.2.0), not exact pinned versions, so two separate npm install runs -- done at different times, or on different machines -- can legitimately resolve to different actual installed versions of a dependency (or one of that dependency's own nested dependencies) if anything compatible was published in between. The first thing to check is whether a package-lock.json file exists in the repo and was actually committed to version control -- that lockfile records the exact, specific version of every dependency in the full tree that was resolved, so installing from it (ideally via npm ci) reliably reproduces an identical install on any machine. If it's missing, or wasn't committed, that's the most likely explanation for a same-package.json-but-different-behavior discrepancy.
questions.professionalAnswer: An identical package.json doesn't actually guarantee an identical install -- that's the thing I'd check first. Most dependencies are declared with a range like ^5.2.0, which lets npm install anything compatible that's been published since, so my install today and my teammate's install next week can legitimately land on two different actual versions underneath, even reading from the exact same package.json. The file I'd check immediately is package-lock.json -- is it actually present in the repo, and was it committed? That lockfile is what pins the exact resolved version of every single dependency, including nested ones, so if everyone installs from it (ideally with npm ci rather than npm install, which respects the lockfile more strictly), the install is reproducible. questions.title: Fix a TypeScript error about a possibly-undefined value
questions.prompt: TypeScript won't compile a function that looks up a transaction by hash in a Map<string, Transaction> and then immediately reads tx.amount, giving an error that tx is possibly undefined. The lookup is inside an if block checking the map has the key. Why does TypeScript still complain, and what's the correct fix?
questions.modelAnswer: TypeScript's control-flow narrowing doesn't automatically connect a separate .has(key) check to a later, independent .get(key) call as proof that the get will succeed -- .get() is typed to always return Transaction | undefined no matter what, and TypeScript has no special-case knowledge tying those two separate map calls together, so it still types the result of .get() as possibly undefined at that call site regardless of the earlier .has() check. The correct fix is to narrow directly on the actual value returned by .get(): store it in a variable and check that specific variable (if (tx) { ...tx.amount... }, or tx?.amount with optional chaining) rather than relying on a .has() check performed on a different expression entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer: The reason TypeScript still complains is that it's not actually reasoning about the relationship between .has(key) and a later .get(key) call -- as far as the type checker is concerned, those are two separate calls, and .get()'s return type is unconditionally Transaction | undefined no matter what happened right before it. The fix is to narrow on the thing I'm actually using: const tx = map.get(key); if (tx) { console.log(tx.amount); }, which lets TypeScript see tx itself has been checked and is no longer possibly undefined inside that block. I'd avoid reaching for a non-null assertion (tx!.amount) just to silence the error -- that tells TypeScript to trust me without TypeScript actually verifying anything, and if I'm wrong at runtime, it fails exactly the way the type system was trying to prevent in the first place.

questions.title: Diagnose a Node/Express server that won't start
questions.prompt: You run node server.js and immediately get Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000. What does this error actually mean, and what are two different ways to resolve it?

questions.title: Diagnose a transaction stuck in pending
questions.prompt: A user submits an Ethereum transaction and it's been sitting as 'pending' for a long time, never confirming. What's the most common reason for this, and what are the two basic ways to get it unstuck?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common cause is that the transaction's gas price (or max fee, under EIP-1559) was set too low relative to what the network currently needs to prioritize it, so validators keep selecting other, higher-paying transactions first while this one just sits in the mempool indefinitely, neither confirmed nor rejected. Two ways to get it unstuck: submit a replacement transaction using the exact same nonce but a higher gas price, which supersedes the stuck one, or send a separate 'cancel' transaction using that same nonce (often a 0 ETH transfer to yourself) with a high enough gas price to get mined first, clearing that nonce so later transactions from the same account aren't blocked behind it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The most likely explanation is that the gas price on that transaction was set too low for current network conditions, so it's technically valid and sitting in the mempool, but every validator keeps choosing other transactions that pay more, leaving this one waiting indefinitely. Just resending the identical transaction again doesn't help -- the stuck one is still sitting there with the same nonce, blocking it. What actually works is either a replacement transaction with that same nonce but a meaningfully higher gas price, which effectively overrides the stuck one, or a dedicated cancel transaction on that same nonce (commonly a 0 ETH send to yourself) with enough gas price to get prioritized and mined first. Either way, the key detail is that it has to use the exact same nonce as the stuck transaction -- that's what actually resolves the conflict instead of just adding a third, separate pending transaction.

Submitting a 'fix' transaction with a different nonce instead of the same one, which doesn't actually replace the stuck transaction

questions.title: Diagnose a Solidity compiler version error
questions.prompt: You try to compile a contract with pragma solidity ^0.7.0, but your project's installed compiler is 0.8.19, and compilation fails. What's actually going wrong, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: The pragma line is an actual constraint the compiler enforces, not just documentation -- ^0.7.0 means 'compatible with 0.7.0 or any later 0.7.x version, but not 0.8.x,' and Solidity 0.8 introduced deliberate, significant breaking changes (most notably default overflow/underflow checks on arithmetic) that the language's designers specifically didn't want applied silently to older code without an intentional decision, so the installed 0.8.19 compiler correctly refuses to compile a file that explicitly declares itself only compatible up to 0.7.x. The fix is either updating the pragma to actually declare compatibility with 0.8.19 (after reviewing whether the contract's logic still behaves as intended under 0.8's stricter arithmetic rules), or installing and using a 0.7.x compiler specifically for this project if there's a real reason it needs to stay on that version.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's going on is that the pragma isn't a comment the compiler ignores -- ^0.7.0 is a real statement that this file is only meant to be compiled with a 0.7.x compiler, and the installed 0.8.19 compiler respects that boundary and refuses rather than guessing it's probably fine. The 0.7 to 0.8 jump specifically changed default arithmetic behavior -- 0.8 added automatic overflow/underflow reverts that 0.7 didn't have -- which is exactly the kind of change where silently compiling old code under new rules could change what the contract actually does, so the compiler won't do that without me explicitly updating the pragma. My fix is updating the pragma to something compatible with 0.8.19, then actually reading through the contract's arithmetic to make sure nothing was quietly relying on 0.7's lack of overflow checks, rather than just widening the pragma range to make the error disappear without checking what changed underneath.
commonMistakes: Treating the pragma version mismatch as a random compiler bug instead of reading what it's actually enforcing
Widening the pragma range just to silence the error without checking whether the 0.7-to-0.8 breaking changes actually affect this contract's logic
Not knowing 0.8 introduced default overflow/underflow reverts, a real behavioral change, not just a syntax update
Assuming any 0.x.y compiler can compile any pragma regardless of the stated version range
keyPoints: The pragma line is an enforced constraint, not a comment the compiler ignores
^0.7.0 is compatible with 0.7.x only, not 0.8.x
Solidity 0.8 introduced default overflow/underflow reverts, a deliberate breaking change from 0.7
Fix: update the pragma (after reviewing arithmetic logic) or install/pin a matching 0.7.x compiler

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the pragma mismatch blocks compilation
Correctly names the 0.7->0.8 breaking change (overflow checks)
Gives a sensible, non-reckless fix

questions.title: Diagnose a compile error on a view function
questions.prompt: A function declared as view fails to compile with an error saying the function changes the state but has the view modifier. Looking at it, it has a single line: balance = balance + 1;. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: view is a declared promise, enforced by the compiler, that a function only reads blockchain state and never modifies it. balance = balance + 1 is a write to a state variable -- it directly changes stored contract state -- which violates that promise, so the compiler correctly refuses to compile it rather than silently allowing a mislabeled function through. The fix is to remove the view modifier entirely, since this function genuinely needs to write state and therefore must be called as a real, mined transaction that costs gas, not a free off-chain read.
questions.professionalAnswer: The compiler isn't being overly strict here -- view genuinely means 'this function will never write state,' and balance = balance + 1 is a write, full stop, so the compiler is correctly catching a function that's mislabeled relative to what it actually does. The fix is simply removing view from this function's signature, since incrementing balance is a real state change that needs an actual transaction -- not a free call -- to happen. I'd also flag that if this had somehow been allowed to compile as view, anyone calling it expecting a free, no-gas read would have been misled about what calling it actually does to the contract's state.
commonMistakes: Assuming view is just an informational hint rather than something the compiler actively enforces
Trying to keep the view modifier and move the write logic elsewhere, rather than recognizing this function genuinely needs to be a state-changing transaction
Not understanding that mislabeling a function as view would mislead callers into expecting a free, no-gas read
Confusing view (no state writes, but can read state) with pure (no state reads or writes at all)
keyPoints: view is enforced by the compiler, not just a comment -- it guarantees no state writes occur
Assigning to a state variable is a write, which violates view
The fix is removing view entirely since this function must be a real, gas-costing transaction
A mislabeled view function would mislead callers about whether calling it costs gas

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the assignment as a state write violating view
Correctly fixes it by removing the view modifier
Explains the consequence of mislabeling a function as view

questions.title: Diagnose sending funds to the wrong address
questions.prompt: A user says they sent test ETH to an address a teammate gave them, but a block explorer shows the transaction confirmed to a completely different address than intended. The addresses differ by a single character. What's the likely explanation, and what tool/practice would have caught this before sending?
questions.modelAnswer: This is almost always a manual transcription error -- a single mistyped or miscopied character somewhere in a long hexadecimal address. Ethereum has no built-in way to reject a transaction just because the destination address 'doesn't exist' or 'wasn't intended' -- any validly-formatted address is accepted and the funds move there with no error at all, and a transaction confirming successfully is not evidence it went to the right recipient, only that it went to a syntactically valid one. The practice that would have caught it before sending: always copy-pasting the full address directly rather than retyping any part of it by hand, and relying on the address's mixed-case checksum encoding, which Ethereum addresses support specifically so a wallet or tool can detect a single-character typo and refuse to send rather than silently sending to a different, equally valid-looking address.
questions.professionalAnswer: The likely explanation is just a manual transcription slip -- somewhere along the way, one character of a long hex address got mistyped or miscopied, and Ethereum has no concept of 'that address doesn't look right' -- any correctly-formatted address is accepted without complaint, confirmed or not, so a confirmed transaction tells you nothing about whether it actually reached the intended person. What would have caught this ahead of time is two things: never retyping any part of an address by hand, always copy-pasting the whole thing, and using the address's checksum -- Ethereum addresses support a mixed-case checksum format specifically designed so that a single flipped character makes the checksum invalid and a wallet can refuse to send rather than happily sending to a typo'd-but-valid address. If the teammate had shared an all-lowercase address with no checksum, that protection wasn't even available to catch the typo in the first place.
commonMistakes: Manually retyping part of an address instead of copy-pasting the entire thing
Sharing or accepting an all-lowercase address with no checksum capitalization, losing typo detection entirely
Assuming a confirmed transaction is proof it reached the intended recipient
Assuming Ethereum validates that a destination address is 'real' or intended, rather than merely correctly formatted
keyPoints: Ethereum accepts any validly-formatted address with no concept of 'intended recipient'
A confirmed transaction only proves it reached a valid address, not the intended one
Always copy-paste full addresses rather than retyping any part by hand
Mixed-case checksum encoding lets wallets detect and reject a single-character typo before sending

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies manual transcription error as the likely cause
Correctly explains that a confirmed transaction doesn't validate intent
Correctly names checksum + copy-paste as the preventive practice

questions.title: Diagnose a failed contract deployment to a test network
questions.prompt: You try to deploy a contract to a public test network through your wallet, and the deployment transaction fails immediately with an 'insufficient funds for gas' error, even though you're sure you have plenty of real ETH in that same wallet on mainnet. What's actually going wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: A wallet's balance is always specific to whichever network it's currently connected to -- mainnet ETH and a given testnet's ETH are two entirely separate balances tracked by two entirely separate networks, even though the same wallet address and the same private key control both. Having real ETH on mainnet does nothing at all for a deployment transaction being sent to a testnet, which requires its own testnet ETH (obtained for free from that testnet's faucet) to pay for gas on that specific network. The fix is confirming the wallet/tooling is actually connected to the intended testnet (not accidentally still pointed at mainnet), and getting testnet ETH from that specific testnet's faucet into the wallet's address on that network before retrying the deployment.
questions.professionalAnswer: The confusion is treating wallet balance as one single global number, when it's actually per-network -- mainnet ETH and, say, Sepolia testnet ETH are two completely separate balances, even though it's literally the same address and the same private key behind both. Having a healthy mainnet balance does absolutely nothing for a deployment going out on a testnet; that deployment needs its own testnet ETH, which I'd get for free from that specific testnet's faucet. My first move debugging this would be double-checking which network my wallet/tooling is actually currently pointed at -- it's an easy thing to leave pointed at mainnet by accident -- and then making sure I've actually gotten testnet ETH into that address on that specific network before trying the deployment again.
commonMistakes: Assuming a wallet's balance is one global number rather than tracked separately per network
Not checking which network the wallet or deployment tooling is actually currently connected to
Assuming testnet ETH from one testnet's faucet works on a different testnet -- each has its own separate faucet and balance
Treating 'insufficient funds for gas' as a code problem in the contract rather than a wallet/network funding issue
keyPoints: Wallet balances are tracked per network; mainnet ETH and testnet ETH are entirely separate
A deployment to a testnet requires that specific testnet's own ETH, obtained from its faucet
Check which network the wallet/tooling is actually connected to before assuming something else is wrong
Different testnets each have their own separate faucet and balance, not interchangeable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains per-network balance separation
Correctly identifies the fix (correct network + faucet funds)

questions.title: Why Node.js can handle many connections on a single thread
questions.prompt: Node.js is famous for handling many simultaneous connections using a single main thread, which sounds like it should be slower than a traditional multi-threaded server. What's the architectural reason this actually works well for I/O-heavy workloads like calling a blockchain node's RPC endpoint?
questions.modelAnswer: Node's architecture hands off I/O operations -- network calls, file reads, timers -- to the underlying system (via libuv) rather than having the single main JavaScript thread sit and block while waiting for each one to complete; the main thread stays free to keep handling other work, and the event loop picks up each operation's callback once that work actually finishes. For something like repeatedly calling an RPC endpoint to check transaction statuses for many users at once, almost all of the real 'waiting' time is spent on the network round trip, not on CPU computation, so a single thread that never blocks on that waiting can comfortably juggle many concurrent requests at once. The architecture's weak point is genuinely CPU-heavy work -- running a heavy computation in a tight loop would actually occupy that one thread and block every other pending operation behind it, which is exactly the kind of workload this model isn't well suited for.
questions.professionalAnswer: The intuition that single-threaded should be slower assumes the thread is actually busy doing work the whole time, and for I/O-heavy workloads, it mostly isn't -- it's waiting on a network response. Node's architecture takes advantage of that: instead of the main thread blocking while it waits for, say, an RPC call to a blockchain node to come back, it hands that waiting off to the underlying system and immediately moves on to other work, coming back only once the response is actually ready. For a scenario like checking many users' transaction statuses, the real bottleneck is round-trip network time, not CPU work, so one thread juggling many in-flight requests at once ends up handling the load just fine. Where this architecture actually falls apart is CPU-bound work -- if I had a function doing heavy cryptographic computation in a loop, that would occupy the one thread directly and block everything else queued behind it, which is the honest limitation of this model.
commonMistakes: Assuming single-threaded automatically means slower, without distinguishing I/O-bound work from CPU-bound work
Believing Node literally executes application code in parallel across multiple threads with no caveat
Not recognizing that genuinely CPU-heavy work would block Node's single thread and undermine this architecture's advantage
Not naming the specific mechanism (I/O handed off, callback queued, event loop picks it up when the stack is clear)
keyPoints: I/O operations are handed off to the underlying system instead of blocking the main thread
The event loop runs queued callbacks once their work finishes and the call stack is clear
This model excels at I/O-bound workloads (like many concurrent RPC calls) where most time is spent waiting on the network
Genuinely CPU-heavy work would block the single thread, which is this architecture's real limitation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the I/O-offload mechanism
Correctly connects it to a concurrent RPC-call scenario
Correctly names the CPU-bound limitation

questions.title: Why break a project into modules with import/export
questions.prompt: Why do JavaScript/TypeScript projects split code across many small files using import and export, instead of writing one large file with everything in it, and what breaks if two modules end up depending on each other circularly?
questions.modelAnswer: Modules let a codebase be organized around single, focused responsibilities -- a wallet module, an API client module, a utilities module -- each exposing only what other code actually needs via export, while keeping its own internal implementation details private. This makes the codebase easier to navigate, to test pieces of in isolation, and to reuse across different parts of the project without copying code around. A circular dependency -- module A imports from module B, and module B also imports from module A -- can produce an incomplete or undefined value on one side, because whichever module finishes initializing first may try to use something from the other module before that other module has finished setting up its own exports; the architectural fix is extracting the logic both modules actually share into a separate, third module that both A and B depend on, rather than having them depend directly on each other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about module boundaries the same way I think about responsibilities -- a wallet module should handle wallet logic, an API client module should handle talking to external services, and each should only expose the handful of things other code actually needs, hiding the rest. That's what makes a codebase navigable instead of one enormous file where everything can reach into everything else. A circular dependency is a real architectural smell, not just a minor bug -- if module A imports from B and B imports from A, depending on which one actually finishes loading first, the other might get an incomplete or undefined version of what it imported, because that module hadn't finished setting up its own exports yet. I wouldn't fix that by just reordering the imports and hoping it resolves itself -- the real fix is pulling whatever logic both modules genuinely need into its own separate module that they can both depend on, so neither one depends directly on the other anymore.
commonMistakes: Putting unrelated logic into one giant file 'to keep things simple,' losing the organizational benefit modules provide
Not recognizing a circular import as the actual cause of a confusing 'undefined' bug at startup
Fixing a circular dependency by reordering import statements rather than extracting the shared logic into its own module
Exporting far more from a module than other code actually needs, eroding the boundary modules are meant to provide
keyPoints: Modules organize code around focused responsibilities, exposing only what's needed via export
This improves navigability, testability in isolation, and reuse across the project
A circular dependency can leave one side with an incomplete/undefined import depending on load order
The real fix is extracting shared logic into a separate module both sides depend on, not reordering imports

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the organizational benefit of modules
Correctly explains what actually breaks in a circular dependency
Gives the correct architectural fix

questions.title: Where TypeScript's type checking actually lives in the build
questions.prompt: If TypeScript's types are erased and don't exist anymore once code is actually running, where in a project's architecture does that type checking actually happen, and what does that mean for a value that arrives from outside the program -- like JSON parsed from an API response?
questions.modelAnswer: Type checking happens entirely at compile time, when the TypeScript compiler (or a tool like ts-node/esbuild) processes the .ts source files and checks them against declared and inferred types before stripping all of that type information out and emitting plain JavaScript; once that compiled JavaScript is actually running, there is no type information left at all for the runtime to check against. This has a real architectural consequence for data coming from outside the program -- a network response, parsed JSON, user input -- because TypeScript can only trust whatever type you (or a library's own type definitions) assigned to that value; if an API actually returns something different from what was declared, TypeScript has no way to catch that at runtime, so genuinely external or untrusted data still needs real runtime validation, not just a type annotation, if the code needs to actually be safe against an API returning something unexpected.
questions.professionalAnswer: The type checking lives entirely in the compile step -- when the TypeScript compiler processes .ts files, checks everything against the declared types, and then strips all of that type information out on the way to producing plain JavaScript. None of it survives into the actual running program; by the time the code is executing, it's just JavaScript with no memory of what types anything was supposed to be. That matters a lot for data coming from outside the program, like a parsed API response -- if I write `const data: UserResponse = JSON.parse(responseText)`, TypeScript is trusting that type annotation completely, it's not actually verifying the parsed JSON really has that shape. If the API changes or returns something unexpected, TypeScript won't catch it, because by the time that data exists, TypeScript isn't watching anymore -- I need real runtime validation, a schema check or similar, for data I don't fully control, not just a type I've asserted onto it.
commonMistakes: Assuming a TypeScript type annotation on parsed JSON is actually verified at runtime, rather than an unchecked assertion
Believing TypeScript provides any safety net at all once the compiled code is actually executing
Not adding real runtime validation for genuinely external/untrusted data despite having TypeScript types for it
Confusing 'the compiler caught this' with 'this is guaranteed true at runtime' for anything originating outside the program
keyPoints: Type checking happens entirely at compile time; types are erased from the emitted JavaScript
Once code is running, there's no type information left for the runtime to check against
A type annotation on external data (like a parsed API response) is trusted, not verified
Genuinely external/untrusted data needs real runtime validation, not just a TypeScript type

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains where type checking actually happens
Correctly explains the consequence for external/untrusted data
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What package.json actually coordinates in a project
questions.prompt: What's the architectural role of package.json in a Node project -- beyond just 'a list of dependencies' -- and why does a project typically also commit a package-lock.json alongside it?
questions.modelAnswer: package.json declares the project's identity (name, version), its entry point and scripts (like a start or test command every contributor can run the same way), and its dependencies as version ranges -- it's the single source of truth for 'what does this project need and how do you run it,' read by npm itself, by CI systems, and by anyone cloning the repository. package-lock.json exists alongside it because package.json's version ranges (like ^5.2.0) are intentionally flexible, and the lockfile instead records the exact, specific version of every single dependency (and every dependency-of-a-dependency) that was actually resolved and installed, so running npm install (or more strictly, npm ci) from that same lockfile reliably reproduces an identical dependency tree on any machine, rather than potentially resolving to slightly different compatible versions over time as new releases get published.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe package.json as the project's coordination file, not just a dependency list -- it's where the entry point lives, where the scripts every contributor runs the same way live (npm start, npm test), and where dependencies are declared as flexible version ranges. The reason package-lock.json sits alongside it is that those version ranges are deliberately flexible, which is great for getting compatible updates automatically but terrible for reproducibility -- two installs done weeks apart could legitimately resolve to different actual versions underneath the same package.json. The lockfile pins the entire resolved dependency tree exactly, down to nested dependencies, so I always commit it and treat npm ci as the command for anything that needs a truly reproducible install, like CI or a fresh teammate's machine.
commonMistakes: Treating package.json as just a dependency list and missing its role defining scripts and project metadata
Not committing package-lock.json, losing exact reproducibility across machines and over time
Editing dependency version numbers by hand in package.json without regenerating the lockfile to match
Using npm install when a reproducible install from an existing lockfile (npm ci) is actually what's needed
keyPoints: package.json defines project identity, entry point, scripts, and dependency version ranges
It's the coordination point read by npm, CI, and every contributor
package-lock.json pins the exact resolved version of the full dependency tree
Committing the lockfile and using it for installs makes installs reproducible across machines and time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains package.json's full coordinating role
Correctly explains why package-lock.json is needed alongside it
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: The client-server shape of a dApp's frontend fetching data
questions.prompt: When a JavaScript frontend calls fetch() to get data from an API, what's actually happening architecturally between the two sides, and why does that same request/response shape apply whether the API is a normal REST backend or a blockchain node's RPC endpoint?
questions.modelAnswer: fetch() sends an HTTP request from the client to a server at some URL; the server processes that request and sends back an HTTP response; the client (asynchronously, since this happens over the network and takes real time) receives and parses that response -- the client never directly touches the server's internals, it only interacts through this defined request/response contract. A blockchain node's JSON-RPC endpoint follows that exact same architectural shape: a dApp frontend sends a request (asking, say, for the latest block number or an account's balance), the node processes it against its own copy of the chain's data, and sends back a response -- the frontend isn't itself running blockchain logic or storing chain data locally, it's a client talking to a server over the network, exactly like calling any other REST API, just using JSON-RPC as the specific request format instead of REST's.
questions.professionalAnswer: The architecture is: client sends a request to a URL, server does whatever work is needed and sends a response back, and the client picks that response up once it actually arrives -- the client never reaches into the server's internals directly, it only ever talks through that request/response boundary. A blockchain node's RPC endpoint is architecturally the exact same shape, which is the part I'd make sure to call out -- when a dApp frontend asks for an account's balance or the latest block number, it's sending a request to a node over the network and getting a response back, it's not running any blockchain logic itself or storing a copy of the chain locally. The protocol details differ (JSON-RPC's specific request format instead of a typical REST API's), but structurally it's the same client-server relationship, and it's just as asynchronous and network-dependent as any other API call.
commonMistakes: Assuming a dApp frontend interacting with 'the blockchain' means it's running blockchain logic locally rather than talking to a node over the network
Not recognizing fetch() calls are asynchronous and need to be awaited/handled like any other promise-based network call
Conflating the specific RPC protocol format with the general client-server architecture, which applies regardless of the protocol
Assuming the frontend has direct access to the chain's data rather than only what a node's response provides
keyPoints: fetch() follows a request-to-server, response-back-to-client architecture over the network
The client never directly accesses the server's internals, only the defined request/response contract
A blockchain node's RPC endpoint is architecturally the same client-server shape, just using JSON-RPC as the format
A dApp frontend is a client talking to a node over the network, not running blockchain logic itself

Correctly connects it to a blockchain node's RPC endpoint
Clarity of explanation
