questions.title: Why a blockchain's node architecture is what makes it decentralized
questions.prompt: A company's normal database runs on servers that company owns and controls. Architecturally, what's actually different about how a blockchain network's nodes are set up, and why does that difference matter for who can alter the data?
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain network is made up of many independent nodes, run by many different, unrelated parties, each one storing and independently verifying its own full (or partial) copy of the exact same ledger -- rather than one organization's servers holding the single authoritative copy of the data. Because thousands of nodes independently hold and check the same data, altering the ledger isn't simply a matter of one party editing their own database -- an attacker would need to successfully alter the data on a majority of the network's independent nodes simultaneously and get the rest of the network to accept that altered version, which is precisely what the network's consensus mechanism is designed to make prohibitively difficult. A block explorer is just a convenient website reading from a node and displaying that shared data in a human-readable way -- it isn't itself the source of truth, it's a window into it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The architectural difference is really about who holds the authoritative copy. A company's database lives on servers that company owns, so they are, by definition, the single source of truth, and can edit it unilaterally. A blockchain network instead has many independent nodes -- run by unrelated parties, with no single owner -- each holding and independently verifying their own copy of the same ledger. That changes who'd actually have to be convinced to alter history: it's not 'ask the one company that owns the database,' it's 'get a majority of thousands of independent, unrelated nodes to simultaneously accept a different version of events,' which is exactly the hard problem the network's consensus mechanism exists to prevent. I'd also be careful to point out that a block explorer is just a website reading from a node -- it's a convenient viewer, not the actual source of truth itself.
commonMistakes: Treating a block explorer's website as 'the blockchain' itself rather than just a viewer reading from a node
Not explaining why many independent copies, rather than just 'more servers run by the same company,' is what actually resists tampering
Assuming decentralization means no one validates data, rather than many unrelated parties independently validating the same data
Describing the difference only as 'no company owns it' without explaining the consensus mechanism's role in enforcing that
keyPoints: A blockchain network is many independent nodes, run by unrelated parties, each independently storing/verifying the same ledger
A centralized database has one authoritative copy, owned and editable by one party
Altering a blockchain's history requires convincing a majority of independent nodes via consensus, not just editing one copy
A block explorer is a viewer reading from a node, not the ledger's source of truth itself

Correctly clarifies the block explorer's role

questions.title: What actually executes when a smart contract function runs
questions.prompt: When Solidity source code gets compiled and deployed, what's actually stored on-chain and what's actually executed when someone calls a function on that contract?
questions.modelAnswer: Solidity source code is compiled down to EVM bytecode -- a sequence of low-level opcodes (the EVM's own instruction set, things like ADD, SSTORE, SLOAD) -- and it's that compiled bytecode, not the original Solidity text, that actually gets stored on-chain at the contract's address. When a transaction calls a function, every node on the network independently loads that same bytecode into its own copy of the EVM (a stack-based virtual machine) and executes the relevant opcodes step by step, each opcode consuming a fixed amount of gas, with every node arriving at the identical resulting state because they're all running the exact same deterministic bytecode against the exact same input; that shared, independently-reproducible execution is what lets the network agree on a contract's resulting state without trusting any single party's computation.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's actually deployed and sitting on-chain isn't the Solidity source code at all -- it's compiled EVM bytecode, a sequence of low-level opcodes that the EVM's instruction set defines. When someone calls a function, every single node on the network independently runs that exact same bytecode through its own copy of the EVM -- a stack-based virtual machine -- executing each opcode and paying its fixed gas cost. The important architectural point is that this execution isn't done once by one trusted party and accepted by everyone else; every node redoes it independently against the same input, and because the bytecode is deterministic, they all land on the identical resulting state without needing to trust each other's computation -- that's what actually lets a decentralized network agree on what a contract call did.
commonMistakes: Thinking Solidity source code itself is what runs on-chain, rather than the compiled bytecode
Not understanding that every node independently re-executes the same bytecode rather than one node computing it and others trusting the result
Conflating the EVM's opcodes with a general-purpose CPU's instruction set, rather than a purpose-built, gas-metered virtual machine
Assuming the Solidity source is retrievable directly from the chain itself, rather than needing to be separately verified/published
keyPoints: Solidity compiles to EVM bytecode, which is what's actually stored and deployed on-chain
Every node independently executes the same bytecode in its own copy of the EVM
Each opcode has a fixed gas cost; total execution cost is the sum of opcodes actually run
Deterministic execution against identical input is what lets the network agree on results without trusting one party's computation

Correctly explains execution across independent nodes

questions.title: Why Ethereum separates read calls from state-changing transactions
questions.prompt: Architecturally, why does Ethereum distinguish between a free, instant 'call' to a view function and an actual gas-costing transaction that changes a contract's state, rather than treating every function call the same way?
questions.modelAnswer: A function that only reads existing state doesn't need to change what every node on the network agrees is true, so it can be answered locally by a single node's own already-synced copy of the data, instantly and for free, without requiring the entire network to reach new consensus on anything. A function that writes state, by contrast, is proposing an actual change to the shared ledger that every node must eventually agree happened -- which requires a real transaction, broadcast to the network, included in a block, and paid for with gas, precisely because reaching that network-wide agreement is the genuinely expensive part. This architectural split -- cheap local reads vs. expensive network-wide writes -- is why a dApp's frontend can constantly display live contract data (via free calls) without charging the user anything, while an actual action, like transferring tokens, always requires a signed, paid transaction.
questions.professionalAnswer: The split exists because reading and writing state are architecturally very different kinds of operations. A read doesn't need the whole network to agree on anything new -- any single node already has the current state and can just answer the question locally and instantly, which is why it's free. A write is different: it's proposing an actual change to the shared ledger, and every node on the network has to eventually agree that change really happened, which means broadcasting it as a real transaction, getting it into a block, and paying gas for the work of reaching that agreement. That's exactly why a dApp can show live, constantly-updating contract data for free through read calls, but the moment a user actually wants to do something -- transfer a token, update a balance -- that requires a signed, paid transaction, because only that goes through the expensive, network-wide agreement process.
commonMistakes: Assuming a view function call still goes through the same consensus/mining process as a real transaction
Not explaining why state changes specifically require network-wide agreement while reads don't
Thinking the gas cost difference between reads and writes is arbitrary rather than tied to what each operation actually requires architecturally
Assuming a dApp frontend displaying live data is itself making paid transactions behind the scenes
keyPoints: Reads can be answered locally by one node's current state, instantly and for free
Writes propose a real change that the whole network must agree happened via a transaction
Gas pays specifically for the cost of reaching network-wide agreement on a state change
This split lets dApps show free live data via calls while real actions require paid transactions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why reads don't require consensus
Correctly explains why writes require a real transaction

questions.title: What the DAO hack and the Merge each actually changed
questions.prompt: The DAO attack and 'the Merge' are both major events in Ethereum's history, but they're architecturally very different kinds of events. What did each one actually involve, at the level of the network's design?
questions.modelAnswer: The DAO attack was a smart-contract-level exploit -- an attacker found and abused a reentrancy vulnerability in one specific deployed contract's own code to drain funds from it, which was a flaw in that contract's logic, not a flaw in Ethereum's own protocol; the network's eventual, highly controversial response (a hard fork to effectively reverse the theft) was a social/governance decision layered on top of a smart contract bug, not a fix to the EVM itself. The Merge, by contrast, was a protocol-level architectural change -- it switched Ethereum's entire consensus mechanism from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake, replacing how the whole network agrees on new blocks, without changing how any individual smart contract's code executes; existing contracts and their logic kept working exactly the same way, because the Merge changed who gets to propose blocks and how, not the EVM that executes contract code.
questions.professionalAnswer: These two sit at completely different layers of the system, which is the distinction I'd lead with. The DAO attack was an application-layer problem -- one specific contract had a reentrancy bug in its own code, and an attacker exploited that bug to drain its funds; Ethereum's own protocol wasn't broken, that one deployed contract's logic was. What happened afterward -- a hard fork to reverse the theft -- was a governance decision the community made in response, not a change to how the EVM works. The Merge is a totally different category of event -- it's a protocol-layer change, swapping out the entire consensus mechanism from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake, which changes who gets to propose the next block and how, but doesn't touch how any individual contract's code actually executes. Every existing contract kept behaving exactly the same after the Merge, because the EVM itself wasn't what changed.

questions.title: What the ABI actually does for an application calling a contract
questions.prompt: A deployed smart contract on-chain is just compiled bytecode with no readable function names left in it. So how does a frontend application actually know how to correctly call a specific function on that contract, with the right arguments, and correctly decode what it returns?
questions.modelAnswer: The ABI (Application Binary Interface) is a separate JSON description -- generated at compile time alongside the bytecode -- that lists every function and event the contract exposes, along with each function's name, parameter types, and return types; it acts as the documented contract between off-chain code and the on-chain bytecode. An application (via a library like ethers.js or viem) uses the ABI to correctly encode a function call into the specific low-level byte format the EVM actually expects, since the deployed bytecode itself has no human-readable names, only numeric function selectors derived from each function's signature, then send that as a transaction or call, and correctly decode the raw bytes that come back into a usable value based on the return type the ABI says to expect. Without the correct ABI, an application has no reliable way to know what to send or how to interpret what it gets back, even though the contract itself is sitting right there on-chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing to get across is that the deployed contract on its own is essentially opaque -- no function names, just bytecode and numeric selectors. The ABI is what makes it usable from outside: a separate JSON file, generated at compile time, that documents every function's name, its parameter types, and its return type. A library like ethers.js or viem reads that ABI to correctly encode a call into the exact low-level format the EVM expects -- turning a human-friendly function call into the right selector and argument encoding -- sends it, and then decodes whatever bytes come back according to the return type the ABI says to expect. If the ABI being used doesn't actually match the deployed contract -- say it's an outdated version from before a redeploy -- calls can get encoded wrong or responses decoded incorrectly, even though the contract itself hasn't changed; the ABI is a separate artifact that has to stay in sync with what's actually on-chain.

Not understanding the ABI is a separate artifact generated at compile time, not something stored on-chain with the contract
Using a mismatched or outdated ABI against a contract, leading to calls being encoded incorrectly or responses decoded wrong
Thinking a library like ethers.js/viem can talk to any contract without needing its ABI at all

Deployed bytecode has no readable function names, only numeric selectors derived from function signatures
A client library uses the ABI to correctly encode calls and decode returned data
A mismatched/outdated ABI against the real deployed contract causes incorrect encoding or decoding

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the deployment script for the staging environment and started testing the rollback path. Today I'm wiring up the health check so a bad deploy gets flagged automatically instead of failing silently. I'm blocked on getting access to the staging server, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real task instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A manager emails you: 'People keep asking me for a status update on deployments by email. How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a team member, I want a dashboard showing current deployment status, so that I can check it myself without emailing the manager.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects a deployment's status within one minute of it changing, with no manual steps' and 'each environment (dev/staging/prod) is shown separately.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a deployment fails. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the manager directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
